topic: The Brachistochrone Problem: The Path of Fastest Descent

sections.title: Introduction: The Challenge
sections.content: Define the problem: Given two points at different heights, what is the shape of the path that allows a bead to slide down in the shortest time under gravity? Introduce the common misconception (the straight line) vs. the truth.
sections.example: A downhill mountain biker deciding between a straight steep drop or a curved ramp.

sections.title: Prerequisite Intuition: Energy and Velocity
sections.content: Briefly review the Law of Conservation of Energy (PE to KE). Visualize that the path must 'spend' time early on to gain velocity quickly, even if it covers more distance.
sections.example: Visual animation of a bead accelerating faster on a steep vertical start versus a gentle slope.

sections.title: The Mathematical Framework: Functional Calculus
sections.content: Introduce the concept of a 'functional'—where the goal is not to find an x, but to find a function y(x) that minimizes the integral of time. Use a visual graph showing the path y(x) and the integral formula.
sections.example: A sliding marble on different wire shapes: linear, circular, and the cycloid.

sections.title: The Solution: The Cycloid
sections.content: Reveal the Brachistochrone curve: the Cycloid. Show the animation of a point on a rolling circle tracing this path. Explain how this specific curve balances distance vs. speed perfectly.
sections.example: An animation of a wheel rolling along a track, tracing the exact path the marble takes.

sections.title: Conclusion and Real-world Application
sections.content: Summarize how this problem birthed the Calculus of Variations. Connect to modern engineering like skate park ramps or roller coaster design.
sections.example: Comparing a 'fastest' roller coaster drop to the geometry of a cycloid.
